title: Punch-needle cushion front
subtitle: A 40 cm square cushion panel worked in punch needle on monks cloth
excerpt: A punch-needle cushion front is worked on monks cloth stretched in a hoop or frame, then assembled with a plain back. The looped pile gives a dense, soft cushion surface. A 40 cm square cushion front takes about 6 hours of punch work at a medium loop height.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional punch-needle textile practice. Punch-needle work on monks cloth is a standard intermediate project widely taught in UK fibre arts and rug-hooking workshops.

glossaryTerms.definition: A hollow needle tool that punches yarn or thread through a backing fabric, forming a loop on the reverse side with each punch. The loops build up into a pile surface.
A plain-weave cotton or linen fabric with an evenly spaced grid structure, used as the backing for punch-needle and rug-hooking work.
The length of each punch-needle loop on the pile side of the work. Adjusted by a dial or gauge on the punch needle tool.

items.name: Monks cloth, cut to 50 cm square (10 cm larger than the finished size on each side)
DK or aran weight wool or acrylic yarn in design colours
Punch needle tool set to 6 to 8 mm loop height
Rug frame or large embroidery hoop, at least 45 cm
Backing fabric and cushion pad, 40 cm square

content.text: Stretch the monks cloth tightly in the rug frame or large hoop. The cloth must be drum-tight: any slack allows the loops to pull back through the cloth on the next punch. Mark the 40 cm square design area in the centre of the cloth with a water-soluble marker. Transfer or draw the design within this area.

Set the punch needle to 6 to 8 mm loop height. Push the needle fully through the monks cloth at the design outline, pull back to form a loop, then move the needle along one thread of the monks cloth grid and punch again. The loops form on the back of the cloth (the pile side); work on the front face. Work the outline of each colour area first, then fill in the interior.

Fill each colour section by working in rows parallel to one side of the monks cloth grid. Space the rows one thread apart. The loops on the back should be dense but not overlapping: if the loops are packed so tightly they push each other sideways, the pile will not stand upright. A consistent row spacing of one monks cloth thread (about 4 mm) is the standard.
Step 4: Secure the work and trim

When the design is complete, apply a thin coat of rug latex or a diluted PVA glue to the back of the cloth across the punched area to lock the loops in place permanently. Allow to dry flat for at least 4 hours. Trim the monks cloth border to 2 cm beyond the design edge.

Place the punched panel pile-side down on a plain backing fabric cut to the same size. Machine or hand sew three sides of the square with a 1.5 cm seam. Turn right side out through the open fourth side, insert the cushion pad, and close the opening with slip stitch.

items.problem: Loops pull back through the cloth when the needle moves to the next punch point
items.cause: The monks cloth is not tight enough in the frame, allowing the cloth to flex and release the previous loop
items.fix: Re-tension the cloth in the frame. The cloth must be drum-tight; if the frame does not hold the cloth firmly, add extra tacks or cord lacing at the frame edges.

items.problem: The pile on the back is uneven with some areas much longer than others
items.cause: The loop height setting was not consistent, or the punch needle was not fully inserted on every punch
items.fix: Check the loop-height dial before starting and confirm that the needle is being pushed fully to the handle on every punch. Partial punches make shorter loops.
